clojure-cli-purifier.summary: Locked, Nix-resolved dependencies for Clojure CLI.

values.language_tooling_setup:
[clojure-lsp](https://clojure-lsp.io) computes the classpath with
`clojure -Spath`, so it reads the locked downloads when the editor's
environment has `.clojure-cli-purifier/bin` first on `PATH`, such as
through direnv. In a project with a `bb.edn`, clojure-lsp asks babashka for
the classpath, and `.lsp/config.edn` points it at `deps.edn`:

```clojure
{:project-specs [{:project-path "deps.edn"
                  :classpath-cmd ["clojure" "-A:test" "-Spath"]}]}
```

clojure-lsp analyzes the jars on the classpath, which hold the Clojure
sources, and needs no other download.
values.quickstart:
nix shell \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#clojure' \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#cli'
clojure-cli-purifier lock \
  --build '-T:build uber' --test '-M:test'
clojure-cli-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/.clojure-cli-purifier/bin:$PATH"
clojure -T:build uber
clojure -M:test

values.language_tooling_setup:
After a prefetch, the packages are in your NuGet package folder and every
project is restored, so a language server that reads a project through
MSBuild (the Roslyn language server, csharp-ls or OmniSharp) works with no
network. Run it with the locked SDK, which `prefetch` links at
`.dotnet-purifier/sdk` next to the lockfile: put `.dotnet-purifier/sdk/bin`
first on its `PATH` and set `DOTNET_ROOT` to
`.dotnet-purifier/sdk/share/dotnet`. Navigation into
a package's code decompiles it locally; source files that SourceLink
downloads need the network.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/dotnet-purifier'
dotnet-purifier lock
dotnet-purifier dotnet build
dotnet-purifier dotnet test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers find `elm`, `elm-test` and `elm-format` on
`PATH`, and the packages through `ELM_HOME`. The tools in
`elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` set `ELM_HOME` themselves, so putting that
directory first on `PATH` is all an editor needs. The same directory holds
`elm-language-server`, which runs the language server with that `PATH`:

```zsh
PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH" code .
```

With direnv, the line `PATH_add elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` in `.envrc`
does the same. The language server sometimes hangs while it starts, and
restarting it from the editor fixes that.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/elm-purifier'
elm-purifier lock
elm-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH"
elm make src/Main.elm
elm-test

tooling API: IntelliJ IDEA, and Eclipse and VS Code through Buildship and

use `.gradle-purifier/distribution` beside the lockfile.

LuaRocks tree. Point the language server at it. For

`prefetch` realizes the rocks, and the language server comes from your own

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor that imports a Maven build, such as VS Code or Neovim through
jdtls, or IntelliJ IDEA, runs a Maven of its own. After a prefetch, make
`.maven-purifier/settings.xml` the editor's Maven user settings,
`java.configuration.maven.userSettings` for jdtls or *User settings file*
in IntelliJ IDEA, and the editor resolves from the locked files without the
network: dependencies, their source jars, and the plugins of its own Maven.

The lock holds the default plugins of the Maven that jdtls embeds, which
the lock run reads from the jdtls of maven-purifier's nixpkgs. An editor whose Maven has other
default plugin versions finds them missing offline, unless the build pins
the version of every plugin it uses in `<pluginManagement>`, as we
recommend; then every Maven asks for the locked versions.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/maven-purifier'
maven-purifier lock
maven-purifier prefetch
mvn test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors such as Metals (in VS Code) and IntelliJ IDEA talk to Mill through
the Build Server Protocol (BSP), and start Mill with the command in
`.bsp/mill-bsp.json`. Write that file through the purifier:

```zsh
mill-purifier mill mill.bsp.BSP/install
```

The command it names is a script under `~/.cache/mill-purifier` that runs
`mill-purifier mill` in the build, so the editor's Mill also runs offline
from the lockfile. The lock run starts Mill's BSP server and asks it what
an editor asks first (the build targets and the sources of their
dependencies), so the server's own libraries and the source jars an editor
shows are in the lock. The script names the mill-purifier package it was
written by; run the install again after updating mill-purifier.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/mill-purifier'
mill-purifier lock
mill-purifier mill core.compile
mill-purifier mill core.test

direnv. The server runs offline.

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers, such as pyright, read the project's virtual
environment, which the offline install fills like any other `poetry
install`. They download nothing.

setuptools installs an editable path dependency through an import hook by
default, which pyright and other type checkers do not follow. This happens
with or without the purifier. Poetry can ask setuptools for its compat mode
instead, which writes a plain path entry, in the project's `poetry.toml`:

```toml
[installer.build-config-settings.<package>]
editable_mode = "compat"
```
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/poetry-purifier'
poetry purifier lock
poetry purifier prefetch
poetry install
eval "$(poetry env activate)"
pytest

An editor imports the build through sbt's build server, and asks it for
the sources of every dependency (`buildTarget/dependencySources`, which
runs `updateClassifiers`). The lock run resolves what a
`dependencySources` request needs: it runs `updateClassifiers` for every
project at its default Scala version, unpublished projects included, and
`updateSbtClassifiers` for the sources of sbt and of the build's plugins.
An editor that imports the build then resolves those sources from the
lock, with the network cut off.

sbt nixLock
sbt compile

scala-cli-purifier.summary: Locked, Nix-resolved dependencies for Scala CLI.

values.language_tooling_setup:
```zsh
scala-cli setup-ide .
```

run through the wrapper, configures Metals, or any other editor that speaks
the Build Server Protocol, to build the project offline on the prefetched
downloads: it points the launch command in `.bsp/scala-cli.json` at the
wrapper, which starts scala-cli's build server with the locked cache and
the offline mirror. Run it again after `lock`.

The lock run opens the project the way an editor does, and compiles it on
the Bloop compilation server that serves an editor, so the lockfile holds
what an editor asks for, such as the source jars of the dependencies and
the compiler bridge of Bloop. `lock --no-ide` locks without them, for a
smaller lockfile.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/scala-cli-purifier'
scala-cli-purifier lock --test
scala-cli-purifier prefetch
scala-cli run .
scala-cli test .

clangd --compile-commands-dir=build

explicit integration rather than silently changing the dependency graph.

cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

installs in the project: TypeScript's language server comes from the
`typescript` package, and ESLint and Prettier come from their own

Yarn's editor SDK, which `yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks` installs; `@yarnpkg/sdks`
then has to be a dev dependency, so that the purifier lockfile records it.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/yarn-berry-purifier#toolchain'

yarn install
yarn run build
yarn test
